To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the abundance of large fish and other marine megafauna in the coastal ocean has declined by orders of magnitude since the advent of industrialized fishing; (2) this decline is the most important cause of ecological changes in coastal ecosystems; (3) the decline in large fish and other megafauna has occurred over a century, and the decline is continuing; and (4) the decline in abundance of megafauna has been associated with a decrease in the abundance of large predators, a

historical overfishing of large consumer species caused a collapse of the structure and function of coastal ecosystems, that time lags were decades or even centuries between the onset of the overfishing and the collapse, and that the collapse was followed by a period of ecological recovery that has not yet been completed in any ecosystem.

(a) overfishing of large consumers has caused the collapse of coastal ecosystems, (b) the collapse of these ecosystems is the most important human-caused disturbance to coastal ecosystems and has been ongoing for centuries, and (c) restoration of coastal ecosystems requires the rebuilding of populations of large consumers to historical levels.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the history of the human interaction with the environment, and the consequences of that interaction for the environment and for the human population.
the history and causes of the collapse of coastal ecosystems, with the goal of providing information for restoration and management.
understanding how the structure and function of ecosystems have responded to the effects of human activities, particularly overfishing, in the past.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
overfishing is the single largest human disturbance to coastal and marine ecosystems and is the cause of the most pervasive human-induced ecological extinction.
overfishing has had a greater effect on the world's coastal ecosystems than any other human activity.
the recent collapse of coastal ecosystems has been caused primarily by overfishing, with the consequent loss of large, predatory fishes and other top consumers.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have demonstrated that historical data provide an essential perspective for understanding ecological changes in coastal ecosystems.

the historical abundance of large consumer species was fantastically large compared to recent observations, and that time lags between the onset of historical overfishing and the consequent changes in the ecological communities of the North Pacific and North Atlantic Oceans were decades to centuries.
the historical overfishing of large consumer species in coastal ecosystems has been so severe that the ecosystems have not been able to fully recover even when overfishing has been halted.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we need to restore ecosystems to a more natural state.
we need to restore ecosystems, not just species.
the historical record shows that the world was once much more diverse and abundant, and that we can return to this state if we are willing to do what it takes.
